deck: 20 Head First Java::02 A Trip to Objectville

cards.front: What is the relationship between a class and an object?
cards.back: A class is a blueprint; an object is one instance the JVM builds from it
cards.extra: The class says what an object of that type will have and can do. A class is not itself an object — it is the instructions for making them, which is why one class can produce thousands of objects.

cards.front: Two objects came from the same class. What do their instance variables have in common?
cards.back: The names and types; the values are independent
cards.extra: Each object carries its own copy of every instance variable, so changing one object's field never touches another's. Three Movie objects can hold three different titles and ratings.

cards.front: Why does a first OO program need two classes?
cards.back: One defines the object type, the other holds main() to create and test it
cards.extra: The tester class has a single job: try out the methods and variables of the new type. Mixing test code into the domain class is what makes small programs hard to grow.

cards.front: In Dog d = new Dog();, what does d hold?
cards.back: A reference to the object, not the object itself
cards.extra: The object is created on the heap; the variable holds the bits the JVM uses to find it. Copying d into another variable gives two names for one dog, not two dogs.

cards.front: How do you reach an object's field or call its method?
cards.back: Through the dot operator on a reference: d.size = 40;, d.bark();
cards.extra: The reference is the remote control; the dot is the button. Fields are assigned, methods are called with parentheses — forgetting them calls nothing.

cards.front: In Head First's terms, what do an object's instance variables and methods represent?
cards.extra: Instance variables hold the object's own data; methods are the things it can do. This split is the mental model behind encapsulation later in the book.

cards.front: What are the two legitimate uses of main()?
cards.back: To test a class, and to launch the application
cards.extra: A test-drive main creates objects and exercises them. Business logic living in main means you never left the procedural world.

cards.front: In a real OO application, what replaces a main() that does all the work?
cards.back: Objects calling methods on each other
cards.extra: The application is a set of collaborating objects; main only starts the first one. If everything still happens inside main, the objects exist but nothing talks.

cards.front: Why does object orientation let you extend a program without breaking tested code?
cards.back: New behaviour goes into new or subclassed classes; existing classes are left untouched
cards.extra: You add rather than edit. That is the claim behind reusable, tested components — the alternative is changing working code and re-testing everything.

cards.front: Where do objects live in memory?
cards.extra: References sit in variables on the stack or inside other objects; the objects themselves are heap allocations, which is why they can outlive the method that created them.
